column5: Only caveat (more drugs today increase addiction, demand and prices in the future) seems insufficient to reverse basic supply-demand result.
column8: The US war on drugs appears to be a total and very costly failure, so alternatives have to be tried and this one seems to have worked well.

column5: See AER paper by Carlos Dobkin and Nancy Nicosi on price effects of the U.S. government's disruption of the methamphetamine market
column8: Marijuana is less dangerous than alcohol. Criminal enforcement for minor marijuana infractions is a waste of societal resources.

column5: Also depends on demand response - may be more consumers if legal, expanding demand - but that seems likely to be smaller than supply effect
column8: Depends on "social costs" and how harms of drug use, effect on crime, policing efforts, tax revenue enter social welfare function.

column5: Price increase isn't only due to risk-- constraints on production, costs of avoiding authority all raise MC.
column8: Too many poorly measured factors to have real certainty about this.
This is an empirical question.  Depends ion how the law affects social acceptance of drugs, whether soft drugs are gateway drugs, etc.

column5: "All else equal" seems to imply something about taxation if legal.
Not sure what is "all things equal," such as demand being constant, taxation of legal drugs, etc.
Illegality leads to high prices and crime.
column8: The current regime of drug enforcement has unacceptably high cost in crime and prison
yes, especially if combined with an anti-drug campaign similar to the campaign against smoking in the U.S.

column5: Supply shifts to the left b/c of a host of factors including paying off authorities and related drug supply restrictions (plus added costs).
column8: Depends on how "moderate" the tax is.
very difficult to judge.  presumably, usage would be higher.  does reduced productivity of users count as a social cost?

column5: I claim no expertise on this subject but the proposition is basic economics
column8: My limited understanding is that there is evidence of harm from cannabis.
The evidence on this is very unclear because many of the consequences are not only hard to estimate, but hard to value.  See Pudney papers..
Have to trade off the costs of the likely extra usage against savings from wasted resources trying to stop the inevitable.

column5: Quantities also adjust because of the effect on demand but the supply price is higher when drugs are illegal.
column8: Two issues confound this. The effect of lower prices and more availability on the young and drug tourism.

column5: Or reduces quality. Presumably illegality also reduces demand, but assuming cost increase is the more relevant & applying Econ 1.
column8: Must be better approaches to drug policy, but don't have an informed view on this one.

column5: I'd imagine that the shorter supply of illegal drugs also makes them more expensive.
Consumers also face risk of punishment, but the evidence is that the effect on suppliers dominates - substantially raising street prices.
column8: Although drug use would increase, the diminished use of violence should yield a net gain.

column5: Basic micro.  Illegality also rules out some efficient forms of production & distribution.
column8: Not at all simple: evidence weak, hard to weight various kinds of costs.

column5: A test of whether the panel is awake.
column8: War on drugs dumber than invading Iraq in search of WMDs. Treat pot like booze. Would also lower prison population.
